I don't think this game is quite what I expected. It's a style of game I'd love to see more of. But while I still mostly enjoyed my time with it, I'm left wanting more.

The story itself is interesting and has enough of those classic thriller movie twist and turns to keep you engaged throughout. Role-playing the "man in the chair" is pretty fun, and you have a few moments that deliver on that promise, at least from a narrative standpoint.

After playing this through once, you'd think the game had multiple endings. You are left wondering if maybe there's some way to correct your mistakes and change the outcome. That is not the case. The ending is pretty bleak, comes pretty quickly (the game itself only being a few hours long at most), and doesn't bring the story to a proper close. I can do without a "good ending", but there's a disappointing lack of closure here.

Broadly speaking, The Operator fails to deliver on the use of "detective skills" it says you'll need in the game's description. You definitely interact with a computer and run a few faux-terminal commands, but most of the time you're just finding a name or a face by clicking the a button that Zoom-Enhances a video CSI style. It sure looks like you're doing the work, but none of it is very challenging and it all feels a little superficial.

There's maybe one section that raises the difficulty and that's because it puts you on a timer and forces you to read an instruction manual. It's the first and only challenging moment the game offers. It was actually a pretty good moment, and the game could have done with a few more scenes this.

I'd not recommend this game to fans of puzzle games who are looking for a challenge, but it's still a fun journey if you want to spend a few hours in the world of a thriller movie. Just don't expect a satisfying ending.

review_text_raw:
I absolutely love this game’s design and idea but sadly I don't think it was executed very well.

Rather than feeling in control of the narrative, most of the game was spent watching the story unfold with little player-contribution. There were different options to choose during conversations, which would somewhat influence the story plot-wise, but given that it's a mystery game and the choice of options available were very limited and surface-level (e.g. will you lie or not lie), replaying it to see what else (if anything) could have happened doesn't feel worth my time.

The story had some small unexpected and exciting twists, however most of these developments were overshadowed by the main plot being very predictable. I think if they had delved more into the individual cases within the game itself and focused less on forming an overarching plot, it would have been much more enjoyable.

The nature of the game put it in a great position to deliver really varied and unique puzzles (e.g. code breaking, crime solving, hacking -- all of which were very fun), yet the quantity of puzzles was seriously lacking. It felt like maybe only an hour out of the 3.5 hours of time spent playing was actually focused on problem-solving and the rest was in tedious over-explanatory conversation. 

I understand this is tagged with visual novel and so maybe the developers intended it for it to be more of a narrative-based experience, but if that is the reason for the lack of puzzles, I would have expected the plot to be more developed and have less of an obvious ending.

review_text_raw:
Played the demo and got really hooked, so I bought the game the next day full price.

AFTER the demo I expected it to be very similar to Orville and Cyber Manhunt, with the primary focus on using the game's mechanics to solve multiple criminal cases, most unrelated or maybe filler and some interconnected into a bigger picture.
It was... kinda like that? But instead of a focus on multiple cases and the solving mechanics, it focuses solely on one storyline.

Which to me was actually really sad I guess because the gameplay mechanics were really well implemented and would have made for a super nice gameplay loop but instead got used once to advance the plot and then got discarded (e.g. the lab analysis or manually unlocking files). 

Also, the game is probably 75% dialogue, in which you are given choices that lead nowhere. You feel like your choices should matter, maybe in resulting in different endings but there is only one ending implemented. It actually made me compare it more to a visual novel than a detective game.

The lack of "filler cases" is also more of a negative in this particular storyline. I've read that the developer wanted to focus more on the main story instead of filler but I think some filler would've helped the player to immerse themselves better into their role, made better usage of the well-implemented mechanics and would've allowed the player to connect with the characters better, settle mentally on the twists and turns of the main story and process them before the next thing gets thrown at them. It felt very fast-paced with no breathing time from basically the get-go and if I'm not mistaken the story takes place within only a couple of days in-game which also does not seem realistic.

Conclusion:
+ well-made from a technical point of view
+ well implemented mechanics
+ good soundtrack
- poor use of mechanics
- unclear advertisement (detective game vs. very story-driven, more of a visual novel)
- no actual choices made by the player even though it feels like they should have mattered
- lack of cases with a rather short gameplay time as a result
- lots of dialogue with comparatively little gameplay

If you're looking for somethin akin to Orville, Cyber Manhunt or even Her Story, this is not it.
I considered requesting a refund but I believe that if I buy a product, receive it and use it, there is no reason in refunding it, even if it was not what I expected

review_text_raw:
I really enjoyed the style of investigation and the way the story was unfolding piece by piece. However, the ending fell flat and painted my overall opinion as negative. None of your actions mattered in any shape or form, there is really only one ending to be had. The choices are just an illusion, all paths lead to the same end. I guess some people like it, but for me this immediately detached all the emotion I had invested to the game and the characters and it felt like I had waisted all that time trying to choose the right path. 

A lot of strings were also left loose, and while it may have been to tease a sequel, it did not feel satisfying. A good game should be it's own complete piece that can enjoyed without digging through a Discord server for additional info or waiting for a sequel to explain everything. 

Another grievance I have with the game lies in the save system; you can't manually save and it only happens automatically at certain checkpoints. This feels extremely outdated and forces you to either play for an unknown amount of time until you hit a checkpoint, or you have to keep starting the day over because your progress isn't saved. Just give people the option to save manually and reload from a checkpoint if they have forgotten what happened. I had to take a 10 month break from the game because the save system made playing feel like a chore - you can't just play for a few minutes (or however long you feel like playing) at a time because your progress could be all for nothing.

I think the game and the developer have a lot of potential and I believe that if the second game fixes all these issues, it can be GREAT.

Cons:

* The bomb defusal mission is just nonsensical. While it's obviously designed and written to be deliberately confusing to challenge the player, it is also ridiculous. The supervisor, Skinner, would be handling this, or at least offering assistance, not just casually leaving another agent's life up to a 3rd day employee who is reading the bomb defusal manual for the first time. Was having a good time in the game up until this mission. If you look at this achievement as well, only some ~50% of players have this achievement, and then you have to wonder, of those 50% how many had to look up a walk-through online in order to complete it? 
* Game was definitely somewhat dry at times where I felt a little bit bored. 
* I won't spoil any specifics but I will say the ending of the game is...not good, in my opinion. 

Pros:

* UI is clean and easy to use. The applications work smoothly without any issues. 
* Gameplay is straight forward and easy to understand. 
* Solid voice acting. 
* Storytelling is pretty engaging. 
* Game very stable, zero crashes or bugs / glitches. 
* No additional DRM beyond Steam.
* No Epic Online Services.

Gameplay Style: Point and click with some typing here and there related to puzzle solving. This requires some research into files on your in-game computer as well as using the provided tools as well. 

Game Length: ~5 Hours or thereabouts. 

Final Rating: 4.5/10. I got the game on sale and puzzle games aren't usually my thing but I wanted to give it a try as it sounded interesting and I like to support indie developers when I can, but this is a game that, despite some story aspects being well-done, the ending soured things for me as well as the bomb defusal mission to the point that I really would not recommend the game to others.

review_text_raw:
This is going to be the oddest negative review I have ever left. This game got me philosophical about reviews: Is a game review to describe whether I think the game is well made? Or is the game review to describe whether I enjoyed it? It's so rare that these two things are out of alignment, I wasn't sure what to write here. I have decided to write a review based on my enjoyment.

So let me just say: This game is well made. It is VERY well made. It's mechanics are a little bit "Papers, Please", a little bit "Clandestine", and a little bit "The Roottrees are Dead" - all meant as a compliment. The production values are top notch. And the story is very well written and very engaging.

And that's where the problem comes in. When a game is this good, my enjoyment hinges on the story being satisfying - and this story is FAR from satisfying. The ending is a cliffhanger that should have been the INTRODUCTION to a game, not a game in itself. And aside from being an incomplete story, the ending is nothing but [spoiler]bad things happening to good people and bad people getting away with it[/spoiler]. And I find that an extremely unsatisfying experience.

So I leave this review to convey an experience for people like me: people who can appreciate a masterfully crafted game that delivers a deeply unsatisfying story. If I'd known how the story ended, I wouldn't have bothered.

review_text_raw:
The Operator is a very short (3 to 4 hours at best) interactive visual novel with good production value. The interface looks clean and easy to use, the voice acting is good, and the interactive elements are pretty decent. For a visual novel. 

It is presented, however, as a game of deduction and puzzle solving. The puzzles and deductions are shallow with too much handholding. As you progress new mechanics are introduced, and then discarded immediately after. This gives the mistaken impression that much more content is waiting for you and puzzles will get more difficult. And then the game is over.

The story is equally shallow. The opening scene reveals too much, making the big reveal at the end something you can piece together within a few minutes of playing the game. The ending is a cliffhanger of sorts, but it makes this game feel like the opening chapter of a larger story that has not been written. Worse is that none of the conspiracy is ever explained, leaving you with many questions that are unlikely to be answered. There are no divergent paths, only one ending, and zero replay value.

If you go into this game expecting a visual novel, you will have an entertaining few hours with an okay story and underwhelming finale. If you go into this game expecting deduction, investigation, and puzzle solving, you will find only disappointment. This ultimately leads to my negative review. For a visual novel it is too short with an unresolved story, and for an investigation game the puzzles are too simple. The Operator has a lot of unmet potential, which is a shame.

A complete disappointment.

1. The gameplay is primitive and boring. Games like Cyber Manhunt or Orwell do this concept much better, in my opinion—they’re more engaging and last longer. The cutscenes drag on, and while you can see why they're there for certain moments... those moments are painfully obvious within the first hour of playing and after that, they seem redundant.
2. The story is shallow and uninteresting. The main twist is something you figure out in the first hour—[spoiler]namely, that your protagonist is Sasha Cole (thanks to the opening scene, the emphasis on Mia COLE, and the fact that your character starts hallucinating when the agent recalls her love for singing). Once you realize that, it’s immediately clear that your friend is the mole, while the "obviously" unfriendly boss is actually a good guy.[/spoiler] This one dumb decision ruins the rest of the game—there’s no wow factor, no payoff.

Why can he effortlessly kill trained agents? What’s the deal with the Organization? The game explains nothing—guess we’ll have to wait for a sequel instead of getting a proper, finished story.[/spoiler]
4. The ending... It left me completely deflated. [spoiler]I hate "everybody dies" endings more than anything, especially when the game tries to pretend it’s being "nonlinear."[/spoiler]
5. It’s very short. Less than three hours to finish.

review_text_raw:
The only thing this kind of game has to do right is to have a compelling story with a mystery that's satisfying to solve, and The Operator fails on that count. I was expecting something like Papers, Please or The Roottrees are Dead but as a murder mystery, but the only part of the mystery that is solved by the end feels more like a side story to the real mystery, which is never solved at all. The plot twists and character developments make little to no sense and seem like the developers first came up with some "cool" moments, which they struggled (unsuccessfully) to tie together.

I will say there ARE some cool moments - there is a [spoiler]bomb defusal scene[/spoiler] which plays out like [spoiler]a singleplayer version of Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes[/spoiler]; I played it with my girlfriend, with her taking notes while I scoured the supplied in-game manual, and it was very hectic and tense and fun. But as with most plot beats in this game, the circumstances that led to that scene made no sense to us and ultimately the outcome didn't seem to change anything important. Despite being such a short game, it doesn't really seem to branch much based on your actions. The Operator doesn't even have multiple endings, and the one ending it does have is both bleak, unsatisfying, and nonsensical.

Combine this with the fact that - in the style of Papers, Please - there is a lot of information at your disposal throughout the game, but the majority of it is never used (such as the fact that every character bio has a set of fingerprints, but they never come up at all) and I'm left with the impression that the developers had much greater plans but just ran out of time/money and decided to release what they had and call it a day.

review_text_raw:
This game only has one ending, and only less than 2½ - 3 hours of content in total, making the cost per played hour very high. 
The one singular ending is quite bad, and even though there are many dialogue options, there are no actual meaningful choices to be made.
There are numerous quite long and somewhat boring unskippable cut scenes. However one could argue that having no skip option is acceptable due to it being somewhat important to pay attention to the them. And since there's only one ending, there's no replayability, and so there's no need to have a skip option. Though realistically, and as others have pointed out, the most probable reason for not having a skip option is to extend the required playtime to over 2 hours so the game cannot be refunded through Steam.
The game has a lot of dialogue, and not a lot of gameplay. What little actual gameplay there is, is enjoyable enough I guess, but also pretty simplistic and easy. This can be seen as both a positive and a negative. If you're looking for any sort of a challenge/puzzle, you will not find it in this game. This game should be definitely thought of as a visual novel more than a puzzle game.
The story itself is mediocre and actually pretty shallow, which is very bad for a game that consists mainly of the story.
The dialogue is fully voice-acted (except for [spoiler]HAL[/spoiler] and the protagonist), which is a definite plus. The voice acting is also pretty high-quality. However I cannot help but feel like way too much developer effort and money was put into the voice acting, when it should've been put into other aspects of the game.
The soundscape and the soundtrack are also good, but really nothing out of the ordinary.

Overall, The Operator is a short, pricey mediocre dialogue-heavy and minimal-gameplay game with high-quality voice acting and heavy hand-holding and railroading, and with only one ending. It feels like the game was designed to be just long enough to make it impossible to refund after reaching the ending (which in fairness one shouldn't do regardless, if they enjoyed the game and reached the ending).

I cannot recommend anything else but to watch someone else such as a YouTuber play this game. I think that will actually add way more to the experience than buying the game and playing it on your own.

Its a very good looking package, with very very shallow gameplay and story.
Almost every mechanic is done better in another game. I'd be fine with that, nothing new under the sun and all, if the game wasn't remarkably short. I think in an attempt to not overstay its welcome, it leaves before it can get interesting at all.
I genuinely think a longer playtime, more cases, and just a bit more meat on the gameplay side would have made this game amazing.
I could look past a lot of that if the story was good too. And it was, at least up until the end. It's nothing new of course, but I wasn't expecting it to be perfect. I enjoyed it, and felt rewarded when I saw the twists coming. Genuenly very fun.
Then, the ending happened. To keep it light on spoilers, its terribly written sequel bait that makes the events of the game you just played literally not matter at all. 
If they had stuck the landing, It would've been fine, but otherwise, its not worth it.
Go play Orwell then Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes, and you'll get a much better time

review_text_raw:
I wanted to love this game but I just cannot recommend you spend money on what is ultimately a disappointing experience. 

The game has a great concept with a strong atmosphere, and what I hoped was great potential but the overall experience ends up feeling disappointingly thin. Reading reviews and looking at the blurb I felt that I was promised tension, deduction, and deeper problem-solving. Unfortunately, it never fully delivers on that potential.

The biggest issue is simply its length. Just as the mechanics start to click and the world begins to feel intriguing, the game is over. It ends before it can build momentum or explore its own ideas in any meaningful way. What could have been a gripping investigation feels more like the prologue to a larger game that never arrives.

The story also ends up predictable. Key beats begin to telegraph themselves early, and the ending lands exactly where you expect it to. Without twists, red herrings, or layers to peel back, the narrative lacks the depth needed to keep you engaged or surprised.

The investigations themselves feel shallow as well. Each case presents a problem, but they’re often solved with just a few simple steps. There’s rarely a need to dig deeper, only once or twice was I cross-referencing clues, or genuinely thinking like an investigator. Instead of complex puzzles or branching deductions, you get straightforward tasks that resolve too quickly to be satisfying.

Overall, The Operator is an interesting idea wrapped in a very short, very predictable package. If you’re looking for a brief atmospheric diversion, it works—but if you want a substantial investigative experience, this one doesn’t reach far enough.
